{{Short description|Measure of association}}
The '''tetrachoric correlation coefficient''' is a measure of [[correlation|association]] between two [[binary data|dichotomous variables]]. It is based on the assumption that the observed binary variables arise by dichotomizing two underlying continuous variables that follow a [[normal distribution]]. The dichotomization may result from measurement design, categorization, or other practical considerations.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |author = Douglas G. Bonett, Robert M. Price |title = Inferential Methods for the Tetrachoric Correlation Coefficient |journal = Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics |date = 2005-06-01 |access-date = 2025-02-08 |issn = 1076-9986 |volume = 30 |issue = 2 |pages = 213–225 |doi = 10.3102/10769986030002213 |url = https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3102/10769986030002213 |language = en|url-access = subscription }}</ref>

The coefficient can be interpreted as the [[Pearson correlation coefficient]] that would be obtained between the two underlying continuous, normally distributed variables if their values were observable.

== Calculation ==
Suppose that the observed values of two dichotomous variables, ''X'' and ''Y'', are summarized in the following 2 × 2 [[Contingency table|contingency table]], where the entries denote cell frequencies:
{| class="wikitable" style="margin:1em auto; text-align: center; background: #FFFFFF;"
|
|''y'' = 1
|''y'' = 0
|total
|-
|''x'' = 1
|<math>a</math>
|<math>b</math>
|<math>a+b</math>
|-
|''x'' = 0
|<math>c</math>
|<math>d</math>
|<math>c+d</math>
|-
|total
|<math>a+c</math>
|<math>b+d</math>
|<math>n</math>
|}
Determining the exact value of the tetrachoric correlation coefficient from sample data requires fairly numerically complex calculations.<ref>{{Cite book |author = Bernard Harris |title = Tetrachoric Correlation Coefficient |date = 2014 |access-date = 2025-02-08 |isbn = 978-1-118-44511-2 |publisher = John Wiley & Sons, Ltd |doi = 10.1002/9781118445112.stat00385 |url = https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781118445112.stat00385 |language = en}}</ref> One must find <math>\hat{\rho}</math> using the following equation:

:<math>\frac{d}{n} = \int_{\hat{h}}^{\infty}\int_{\hat{k}}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2\pi\left(1-\hat{\rho}^2\right)^{1/2}}\text{exp}\left[\frac{-\left(x^2-2\hat{\rho}xy+y^2 \right)}{2\left(1- \hat{\rho}^2 \right)}\right]dy\text{ }dx</math>,

where <math>\hat{h} = \Phi^{-1} \left( \frac{a+c}{n} \right)</math> and <math>\hat{k} = \Phi^{-1} \left( \frac{a+b}{n} \right)</math>.

In 2005, Bonett and Price proposed a simplified formula that yields an estimate with good properties<ref name=":0" />:

:<math>\hat{\rho}^{*} = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{1+\hat{\omega}^{\hat{c}}}\right)</math>,

where: <math>\pi</math> is [[Pi|the number π]], and <math>\hat{c}</math> is determined by the following formula:

:<math>\hat{c} = \frac{1}{2} \left(1-\frac{|b-c|}{5(n+2)}-\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\min(a+b;a+c;b+d;c+d)+1}{n+2}\right)^2\right)</math>

and <math>\hat{\omega}</math> is an estimate of the [[odds ratio]] using the contingency table cell counts increased by 0.5:

:<math>\hat{\omega} = \frac{(a+0.5)(d+0.5)}{(b+0.5)(c+0.5)}</math>.
